extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing MPEP eligibility guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the Step 2A Prong One abstract-idea inquiry under U.S. patent law (MPEP §2106.04): identifying whether claim limitations recite an abstract idea by mapping them to enumerated groupings and then proceeding to Prong Two when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners' Step 2A Prong One identification procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should (1) identify the specific claim limitation(s) that the examiner believes recite an abstract idea, and (2) determine whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the enumerated abstract-idea groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea at Step 2A Prong One and proceed to Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional claim elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (MPEP §2106.04(d)). If the identified limitation(s) do not fall within any grouping, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the eligibility analysis at Step 2A Prong One ends (Pathway B), unless the claim recites another judicial exception (law of nature or natural phenomenon). Examiners should identify at least one grouping, and preferably all applicable groupings, if a limitation falls into multiple groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated abstract idea groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas are organized into three enumerated groupings: (1) Mathematical concepts (relationships, formulas/equations, calculations); (2) Certain methods of organizing human activity (fundamental economic principles/practices; commercial or legal interactions; managing personal behavior/relationships); and (3) Mental processes (concepts performed in the human mind such as observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These groupings are rooted in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent and are intended to shift examiners from a strict case-comparison approach to applying an organized body of case law across technologies and claim types. Groupings are not mutually exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts grouping (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations. The courts have repeatedly identified these as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a claim recites a mathematical concept, consider whether the claim actually recites the mathematical concept or merely is based on or involves one. A limitation merely based on or involving a mathematical concept may not fall into this grouping if the mathematical concept itself is not recited in the claim. A mathematical concept need not be expressed in symbols; textual wording (e.g., 'determining a ratio of A to B' or 'calculating the force by multiplying mass by acceleration') can recite a mathematical concept. Cite and consider relevant cases such as Benson, Flook, Diehr, Bilski, Thales Visionix, SAP America v. InvestPic, Digitech, and Bancorp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical relationship is a relationship between variables or numbers that may be expressed in words or as an equation (e.g., pressure = F/A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Arrhenius relationship between reaction rate and temperature (Diamond v. Diehr), conversion between binary-coded decimal and pure binary (Benson), relationships between antenna conductor arrangement and radio activity (Mackay Radio), and organizing/manipulating information through mathematical correlations (Digitech). Such relationships recited in a claim support classification in the mathematical concepts grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas or equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a numerical formula or equation, or a textual equivalent of a formula (e.g., 'determining a ratio of A to B'), fall within the mathematical concepts grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: explicit equations (Arrhenius equation), formulas for computing alarm limits (Parker v. Flook), formulas for hedging (Bilski). Textual descriptions of formulas (e.g., 'calculating F = m*a') should be treated as formula recitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical calculation is an operation (e.g., multiplication, exponentiation) or act of calculating using mathematical methods to determine a variable or number. Claims reciting such calculations (interpreted broadly in light of the specification) are within the mathematical concepts grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single word is required to indicate a calculation; terms like 'determining' or 'performing' may encompass calculations. Examples include resampled statistical analysis (SAP America v. InvestPic), calculating alarm limits (Flook), converting coordinates, managing insurance policy values (Bancorp), algorithms to determine optimal visits (In re Maucorps), and calculating differences between data values (In re Abele).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity (grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: This grouping covers concepts relating to (a) fundamental economic principles or practices; (b) commercial or legal interactions; and (c) managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people (including social activities, teaching, following rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The qualifier 'certain' limits the grouping: not all organizing-activity methods are abstract ideas (e.g., a defined set of steps for combining ingredients to create a drug formulation is not). The grouping is limited to the enumerated sub-groupings and should not be expanded except in rare circumstances. The number of people involved is not dispositive; the inquiry is whether the activity itself falls within a sub-grouping. Examples are drawn from Alice, Bilski, and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic principles or practices (subgroup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes economic/commercial concepts such as hedging, insurance, mitigating risk, price optimization, and other practices concerning the economy and commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'fundamental' does not require the practice to be old or well-known; new methods can be fundamental economic practices (e.g., a new price optimization method). Case examples: hedging (Bilski), intermediated settlement (Alice), managing stable-value life insurance policies (Bancorp), offer-based price optimization (OIP Technologies), local processing of payments (Inventor Holdings), placing orders based on market info (Trading Technologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions (subgroup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that effectively recite transactional or contractual relationships or other commercial/legal interactions are likely within this subgroup. Example: a transaction performance guaranty (contractual relationship) as in buySAFE v. Google.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior or relationships (subgroup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Covers activity involving personal behavior management, relationships, and interactions between people, including social activities, teaching, and following rules or instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subgroup can encompass single-person activities (e.g., following a set of instructions on a device) or multi-person interactions (e.g., online loan shopping). Determination should focus on the nature of the activity relative to the subgroup rather than the number of participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as concepts performed in the human mind (including observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting purely mental steps or concepts that can be performed in the mind fall into this grouping and may be treated as abstract ideas under Alice and related precedent. Consider whether the claim limitations are merely mental concepts or whether they are integrated into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of claims that do not recite abstract ideas (non-limiting examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain claims do not recite an abstract idea even if they are based on or involve an abstract idea; such claims are eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting hypothetical examples provided: i) a printer with belt, roller, printhead and ink cartridge; ii) a washing machine with tub, drive motor, controller, housing; iii) an earring sensor for blood glucose with memory; iv) a method for sequencing BRCA1 gene sequences via PCR and sequencing; v) a method for loading BIOS into a local computer from remote memory; vi) a method of rearranging GUI icons based on usage metrics tracked via processor memory allocation; vii) a method of training a neural network with staged training sets and transformations. The Step 2A Prong One analysis requires a claim to 'recite' (set forth or describe) an abstract idea before proceeding to Prong Two; mere involvement or basis on an abstract idea is not sufficient to find the claim recites an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling claims that implicate multiple judicial-exception groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims can recite limitations that fall within more than one abstract-idea grouping or sub-grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claim limitations fall within multiple groupings, examiners should identify at least one grouping and preferably identify all applicable groupings before proceeding with the Step 2A Prong Two analysis. Example: performing mathematical calculations using a formula that could also be performed in the human mind may fall within both the 'mathematical concepts' and 'mental process' groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting other judicial exceptions (laws of nature/natural phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites another judicial exception (e.g., a law of nature or a natural phenomenon), the examiner should consult the relevant MPEP sections for Step 2A analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2106.04(b) and 2106.04(c) for guidance on claims that recite laws of nature or natural phenomena. The abstract-idea grouping analysis is specific to the abstract-idea judicial exception; other exceptions require their own analysis.
